title: Reimagining Transfer Agent with Blockchain at the Centre
content:
One of the most significant regulatory shifts in modern securities history is being built quietly beneath the headline noise of crypto price swings. 

The role of the transfer agent,  a function foundational to capital markets that most investors never think about, is about to be rewritten, and blockchain is the instrument of that rewrite.

On February 18, 2026, [When Security Exchange Comission](https://www.sec.gov/) (SEC) Chairman Paul S. Atkins stood at ETHDenver, alongside Commissioner Hester M. Peirce, he confirmed what institutional infrastructure professionals had been watching for: a transfer agent modernisation rulemaking that will formally accommodate the role of blockchain in securities recordkeeping. This single line, buried in a broader regulatory agenda preview, may carry more long-term operational weight than any other announcement made that day.

This article unpacks what it means, why it matters, and what institutions should be doing about it now.

## What a Transfer Agent Actually Does and Why It Matters for Tokenization

Before examining what is changing, it is worth being precise about what a transfer agent is, because the function is often misunderstood outside of operations and compliance teams.

A registered transfer agent is the legal custodian of the [shareholder register](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/shareholder-register.asp). Under the [Securities Exchange Act of 1934](https://www.nyse.com/publicdocs/nyse/regulation/nyse/sea34.pdf), any entity that maintains the official record of who owns a security and processes changes to that record, is performing transfer agent functions and must be registered with the SEC. The role covers:

- Maintaining the authoritative ledger of security ownership

- Processing the transfer of securities between parties

- Handling dividend and distribution payments to shareholders

- Managing corporate actions; splits, mergers, conversions

- Issuing and cancelling certificates or book-entry positions

- Reconciling the share register with depositories such as the Depository Trust Company

In the traditional system, this function sits between the issuer and the depository. The transfer agent holds the "golden record" of who owns what. Every transfer, every distribution, every corporate action flows through this function.

Now consider what a blockchain does in a tokenized securities environment. It maintains an authoritative, time-stamped, tamper-evident record of ownership. It processes transfers automatically via smart contract. It can execute distributions programmatically. It manages corporate actions through on-chain governance logic. It issues and burns tokens in place of certificates.

In other words, a blockchain-based tokenization platform performs transfer agent functions by definition, and in law. And under current US securities regulations, any entity doing so must be a registered transfer agent with the SEC, regardless of the technology used (SEC, Exchange Act Section 17A). This is the legal reality that the transfer agent modernisation rulemaking is designed to address.

## The Gap the Rulemaking Is Closing
The current transfer agent regulatory framework was written for a world of paper certificates and batch-processing mainframes. It has been updated incrementally over the decades, but its core architecture assumes a centralised recordkeeper operating within a traditional custodial chain.That architecture creates three fundamental friction points when applied to blockchain-native security infrastructure.

First, the rules assume a single, identifiable recordkeeper. On a distributed ledger, the record is maintained collectively across nodes. There is no single party "holding" the register in the traditional sense. Existing rules do not map cleanly onto this model, creating ambiguity about who bears regulatory responsibility.

Second, the rules were not designed for programmable compliance. Current transfer agent obligations include manual processes approval workflows, paper-based reconciliation, batch settlement reporting that are rendered redundant when compliance is encoded directly into the smart contract. The rules require an entity to perform functions that the technology performs automatically. This creates duplication, cost, and legal uncertainty.

Third, the equivalence question is unresolved. Under current law, a directly registered shareholder (whose name appears on the issuer's register held by the transfer agent) and a beneficial owner (whose position is held via [DTC](https://www.dtcc.com/about/businesses-and-subsidiaries/dtc) and a broker) have different legal standings, different rights, and different information entitlements. For tokenized securities held on-chain, it is not yet legally settled where in this hierarchy the holder sits or whether a new category needs to be created entirely. 

## What the New Propositions Are Expected to Establish

Based on the SEC's stated agenda, the [DTCC](https://www.dtcc.com/) pilot framework,[ Ondo Finance](https://ondo.finance/)'s formal submission to the Crypto Task Force, and the broader direction of the Commission's tokenization work, modernisation rulemaking is expected to introduce several new propositions for transfer agent licensing and operations.

 A. <u>A Blockchain-Native Registration Pathway</u>

The rulemaking is expected to create a formal pathway for entities operating blockchain-based recordkeeping systems to register as transfer agents with the SEC on terms that reflect how distributed ledger technology actually works, rather than forcing a blockchain onto legacy compliance obligations designed for centralised systems.

This would mean a new class of registered entity: the tokenization agent or digital transfer agent;  a licensed infrastructure provider whose primary function is maintaining authoritative on-chain ownership records for tokenized securities. Chairman Atkins specifically referenced this framing at ETHDenver, noting that issuers wanting to tokenize their securities could "work with a transfer agent or other tokenization agent to tokenize their securities so that they can be traded onchain."

The creation of this formal category is significant. It provides regulatory clarity for platforms that have been operating in ambiguity, and it opens a licensed institutional market for blockchain-native recordkeeping that does not currently formally exist in US securities law.

 B. <u>Legal Equivalence Between On-Chain and Book-Entry Ownership </u>

One of the most consequential expected propositions is the establishment of legal equivalence between tokenized share ownership and traditional book-entry positions held via DTC.

Currently, direct registration (name on the issuer's register) and beneficial ownership (held via DTC and broker) carry different legal rights. For tokenized securities, it has not been legally settled whether holding a token representing a share is equivalent to direct registration, beneficial ownership, or something else entirely.

Ondo Finance's submission to the SEC's Crypto Task Force made this point with precision, noting that the transfer agent modernisation rulemaking should "level the playing field and create greater equivalence between holding shares in directly registered forms and beneficial ownership forms" which, once achieved, would mean that tokenized shareholders have the same rights, access to information, and legal standing as shareholders in the traditional system

This equivalence is not a technical detail. It is the legal prerequisite for tokenized securities to be held, traded, and managed by institutions without legal uncertainty about the rights they are acquiring.

 C. <u>Programmatic Compliance as a Valid Discharge of Transfer Agent Obligations</u>

A third expected proposition is the formal recognition that smart-contract-encoded compliance can satisfy transfer agent obligations rather than requiring a licensed human intermediary to manually execute functions that the technology already performs automatically.
According to Chairman Atkins at ETHDenver: "One interesting aspect of technology is the ability to embed compliance into the smart contract code. A company's founders, for example, could code their commitment not to resell their securities for a certain period of time into the smart contract governing tokenized securities."

If regulators formally recognise that a smart contract performing transfer agent functions; maintaining the register, processing transfers, enforcing restrictions; constitutes a valid, compliant discharge of those obligations, the cost and complexity of operating tokenized securities infrastructure changes materially. The compliance layer is not overhead added on top of the transaction. It is the transaction itself.

This proposition also has significant implications for privacy. Zero-knowledge proof technology could allow AML and Bank Secrecy Act compliance to be verified without requiring individuals to disclose their full financial history to intermediaries. A development in which the newly launched privacy-preserving version of the [CMTAT](https://cmta.ch/standards/cmta-token-cmtat) framework has already begun to demonstrate in production. A registered digital transfer agent could potentially verify investor eligibility and compliance status on a cryptographic basis without holding or transmitting private financial data in the traditional sense.

## Accommodation of Permissionless and Permissioned Blockchain Environments

The rulemaking is also expected to address the distinction between permissioned and permissionless blockchain environments; a distinction that carries significant implications for how institutional-grade transfer agent functions are structured.

Atkins stated clearly that "market participants should be able to engage with decentralised applications on public, permissionless blockchains if they desire" . This is a meaningful signal that rulemaking will not restrict transfer agent functions to private, permissioned chains controlled by a single institutional operator, but will instead create a framework accommodating both environments, with appropriate safeguards for each.

For institutions, this opens the possibility of operating transfer agent functions on major public networks with regulatory backing rather than being confined to proprietary chains with limited interoperability and liquidity.


## What Institutions Should Be Doing Now 

The regulatory direction is clear. For institutions operating in or adjacent to the tokenized securities space, three actions are immediately relevant.

- Assess your transfer agent exposure: Make sure that any platform, custodian, or infrastructure provider that maintains records of tokenized security ownership or that processes transfers of such securities are likely performing transfer agent functions under 
existing law. Understanding your current regulatory position ahead of rulemaking is essential.

- Map your infrastructure against the expected framework: The new propositions will reward institutions that have already built blockchain-native recordkeeping systems with compliance logic embedded at the protocol level. Institutions still operating tokenized securities on top of legacy transfer agent architecture will face a more complex transition. Sereel builds precisely on this architecture. Rather than treating compliance as a separate operational layer applied, Sereel embeds regulatory logic directly into the financial infrastructure itself.

- Engage the regulatory process: The SEC has been explicit at across multiple task force roundtables that it welcomes input from builders and institutions. The rulemaking process will have a public comment period, and the technical specifics of the final rules will be shaped, in part, by the quality of institutional engagement during that window.

## Conclusion

The transfer agent has been an invisible backbone of capital markets for nearly a century. The coming modernisation rulemaking does not eliminate that function;  it elevates it. By creating formal licensing pathways for blockchain-native recordkeeping, establishing legal equivalence between on-chain and traditional ownership, and recognising programmatic compliance as valid, the SEC is laying the foundation for a securities market infrastructure that is faster, more transparent, and more accessible than anything the current system makes possible.

This is where the long game in tokenization is actually being played, not in price charts, but in ownership records, compliance architecture, and regulatory licensing frameworks that will govern how capital moves for the next several decades. The infrastructure needs to be right. The frameworks to make it right are being written now.

title: Sereel Becomes a Validator on Canton Network
content:
$8 trillion in on-chain assets, approximately $350 billion in daily repo activity and over 600 validators securing synchronized financial workflows. This is the operational footprint of Canton Network today; a smart contract network built for regulated financial markets. On February 22, 2026, Sereel officially became a validator on the Canton Network. Canton’s architecture directly addresses two constraints that have historically limited institutional adoption of blockchain infrastructure: rigid transparency models and shared throughput bottlenecks. Sereel’s objective as a validator is clear:serve as an application provider that enables financial institutions to issue tokenized assets on Canton through its platform, while also offering node-as-a-service infrastructure. ## Understanding the Validator Participation Within the Canton Network The Canton Network was built to address two structural limitations that have constrained enterprise blockchain adoption. 1. Most smart contract networks require applications to inherit the governance structure and fully transparent privacy model of the underlying chain. For financial institutions, this creates unacceptable trade-offs between openness and confidentiality 2. Applications on shared public chains compete for transaction throughput. Congestion in unrelated use cases can impact settlement finality and cost predictability — an operational risk that regulated markets cannot tolerate. Canton’s architecture resolves both constraints. It operates as a network of networks. Independent applications can define their own privacy rules, governance structures, scaling parameters, and permissions while remaining interoperable within a broader synchronized ecosystem. Instead of competing for throughput on a single shared ledger, applications operate in coordinated but independent sub-environments, connected through a shared synchronization layer. This synchronization layer, supported by a decentralized group of validators, ensures that transactions can settle atomically across institutions without exposing unnecessary data. Execution, ownership, privacy, and compliance all operatig within this shared framework. Within this architecture, validators are not symbolic participants. They secure, verify, and maintain the integrity of synchronized execution across the network. By becoming a validator, Sereel participates directly in the network’s trust and synchronization layer. At the same time, Sereel serves as an application provider enabling institutions to issue tokenized assets through its platform. ## Canton’s Architectural Advantage and Why Sereel Aligns With It The current phase of tokenization isn’t about whether assets can be tokenized or not, it’s about whether tokenized assets can operate inside regulated capital markets without introducing structural risk. Canton’s advantage lies in its synchronization model which includes: 1. Privacy Without Isolation: Public networks enforce transparency by default. While transparency is a strength in open ecosystems, it is often incompatible with financial confidentiality requirements. Canton enables programmable privacy at the application level. Data is visible only to authorized participants, while synchronization ensures consistent state across institutions. This architecture allows institutions to transact without exposing sensitive balance sheet or counterparty information to unrelated participants. For financial institutions, privacy is not optional. It is regulatory and competitive necessity. 2. Governance Independence Traditional smart contract environments impose shared governance models across all applications. Financial institutions are unlikely to accept governance decisions driven by unrelated token holders or external communities. Canton allows each application to define its own governance framework while remaining connected to the broader network. For banks, asset managers, and broker-dealers, this means they can maintain internal compliance structures and jurisdictional alignment while benefiting from synchronized settlement. 3. Throughput Isolation and Operational Predictability: Financial institutions require deterministic settlement and predictable cost structures. Networks where unrelated activity affects transaction performance introduce systemic risk. Canton isolates application throughput while preserving synchronization. This means a financial institution issuing tokenized deposits or equities is not exposed to congestion risk from unrelated network activity. Consider a bank in Kenya mints tokenized deposits on Canton. These deposits represent legally recognized liabilities recorded within a synchronized ledger. The bank uses these tokenized deposits as collateral for an overnight loan from another Kenyan bank. The transaction must meet several requirements: - Confidentiality of balance sheet positions - Compliance with local regulatory frameworks - Atomic settlement of collateral and liquidity - Clear audit trail - Legally enforceable ownership representation On a traditional public chain, confidentiality constraints would create friction. On isolated private ledgers, interoperability would be limited. On Canton, the two banks can execute synchronized, atomic settlement using programmable privacy controls. The transaction finalizes without exposing sensitive data beyond the authorized parties. Compliance controls are embedded. Settlement risk is minimized. Sereel’s role is to act as the enabling layer, providing the application interface and infrastructure that allow the banks to mint and manage tokenized deposits securely. ## What Validator Status Enables for Sereel and Its Clients 1. Infrastructure Credibility Institutions evaluating tokenization partners conduct infrastructure due diligence. They assess whether service providers are merely building user interfaces or whether they are embedded in the network’s operational layer. By operating a validator on the Canton Network, Sereel demonstrates direct participation in securing and synchronizing the network. This reduces counterparty perception risk. It signals long-term alignment rather than opportunistic integration. 2. Node-as-a-Service Integration: Many institutions lack the internal expertise or desire to manage blockchain infrastructure directly. Yet they require controlled environments that align with compliance frameworks. Sereel’s model addresses this gap. Through node-as-a-service offerings, institutions can: - Operate within Canton’s synchronized environment - Maintain controlled participation parameters - Integrate blockchain infrastructure with internal systems - Ensure privacy configurations align with regulatory expectations.

Validator participation deepens Sereel’s technical proximity to the network’s core synchronization layer, strengthening its ability to deliver these services reliably. 3. Strategic Optionality Across Chains: Sereel is not restricting itself exclusively to Canton. It intends to hold positions on other chains while enabling clients on Canton. This multi-chain posture creates strategic flexibility. Canton serves as the institutional synchronization layer for privacy-sensitive and regulated use cases. Other chains may serve different asset classes or liquidity environments. By anchoring institutional tokenization capabilities on Canton while maintaining cross-chain presence, Sereel avoids single-network dependency. Validator participation ensures deep alignment where institutional-grade privacy and synchronization are required most. The evolution of tokenization is moving away from isolated token platforms toward synchronized financial infrastructure. Canton represents a structural response to institutional constraints: privacy, governance autonomy, throughput isolation, and atomic settlement. Its scale; trillions in assets, hundreds of billions in daily activity, and a broad validator base is a sign that synchronized execution across institutions is no longer theoretical. Sereel’s validator participation reflects recognition that long-term value in tokenized markets will accrue not only to those who build applications, but to those aligned with synchronization layers. For organizations that want to tokenize information-sensitive assets within small, regulated investor pools, the question is no longer “Can we tokenize?” It is “On which architecture can we do so without compromising privacy, compliance, or operational control?” ## Conclusion Sereel becoming a validator on the Canton Network signals strategic alignment with institutional-grade infrastructure. Canton’s architectural advantage including privacy programmability, governance independence, throughput isolation, synchronized execution, and embedded compliance, addresses the core constraints that have limited enterprise blockchain adoption. Sereel’s role is to enable institutions to operate within that architecture: issuing tokenized assets, managing nodes, and participating in synchronized capital markets without sacrificing confidentiality or regulatory alignment of its clients. In an environment where infrastructure determines durability, alignment with the synchronization layer is not incremental. Sereel is building the operational and application layer that allows institutions privately and securely tokenize in alignment with regulatory frameworks.

title: HOW Bitcoin is Related to Traditional Market
content:
In March 2020, Bitcoin Crashed With Wall Street

It fell nearly 50% in a single day, and at the same time, U.S equities triggered circuit breakers, The [S&P 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%26P_500) was in free fall. The [Nasdaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdaq) composite was collapsing. Global markets were seizing.

For years, Bitcoin had been marketed as independent, uncorrelated, anti-establishment, and hedge against the financial system. Yet in the moment of peak stress, it fell with the SYSTEM. That day revealed something uncomfortable but important:

Bitcoin was no longer outside traditional markets. It had already become part of them.
This relationship did not emerge overnight. It formed gradually, through liquidity cycles, derivatives infrastructure, institutional wrappers, and macroeconomic forces that now bind Bitcoin and the traditional market together.

In this article, we will examine how Bitcoin evolved from a digital experiment into a macro-sensitive financial investment tool that now moves alongside traditional markets.

## The Isolation Era

Between 2009 and 2016, Bitcoin functioned largely within its own speculative ecosystem. Before the first halving in November 2012, miners produced roughly 3,600 BTC per day. After that, issuance dropped to about 1,800 BTC per day. By the second halving in July 2016, issuance would fall again to 900 BTC per day.
During this period:

- Institutional custody was virtually nonexistent.

- There were no regulated futures markets.

- Liquidity was concentrated on crypto-native exchanges.

- Correlation with the S&P 500 was statistically weak and inconsistent.

Price movements were driven by development changes, investors sentiments, industry headlines, and internal crypto speculation. Bitcoin was volatile but not macro-sensitive. A Federal Reserve meeting did not move Bitcoin. Treasury yields did not dictate its direction and even in developing continent like Africa, Bitcoin’s pricing was largely determined by global speculative cycles rather than local economic fundamentals. It remained globally disconnected from traditional capital markets.

In its early years, Bitcoin functioned largely in isolation. However, this changed in 2017


## The Moment Bitcoin Entered Financial Infrastructure

On December 18, 2017, the [Chicago Mercantile Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Mercantile_Exchange) launched Bitcoin futures. An event that marked a structural turning point for Bitcoin. Until that moment, Bitcoin was largely traded on crypto-native exchanges. Participation was dominated by retail investors, early adopters, and a handful of specialized funds willing to navigate fragmented liquidity and limited regulatory clarity. Price discovery happened in an ecosystem that traditional finance observed from a distance.

What the launch meant was that institutions could gain regulated exposure without directly holding Bitcoin. A pension fund, hedge fund, or asset manager no longer needed to custody private keys or onboard offshore exchanges. They could trade Bitcoin exposure through a familiar derivatives venue, under established clearing rules, margin requirements, and compliance standards.

This shift accomplished several things simultaneously.it connected Bitcoin to traditional capital management strategies. This institutionalization did not instantly make Bitcoin move in lockstep with equities. However, it laid the groundwork for macro sensitivity. 

Once Bitcoin was accessible through regulated derivatives, it became easier for capital to flow in and out based on broader market conditions. Bitcoin was no longer just a technological experiment or speculative token. It had entered the architecture of traditional finance.
The CME futures launch did not simply create a new trading product. It created a bridge. And once that bridge existed,the capital could move across it 


## The Liquidity Shock That Changed Everything

When Bitcoin dropped nearly 50% in March 2020, falling from around $7,900 to below $4,000, affecting the traditional market, investors across asset classes sold what they could; equities, commodities, emerging market and digital assets to raise the U.S. dollars, and this is where policy intervention came in.

On March 23, 2020, the [Federal Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve) announced unlimited quantitative easing. The scale was unprecedented:

- February 2020: Federal reserve balance sheet ≈ $4.2 trillion

- June 2020: ≈ $7.1 trillion

- Peak in April 2022: ≈ $8.96 trillion

Liquidity did not just return, it surged. Bitcoin’s move was even more dramatic. From roughly $3,800–$4,000 in March 2020, it rose to approximately $69,000 by November 10, 2021; a gain of over 1,600%.

During extended stretches of 2020 and 2021, a 90-day rolling correlation between Bitcoin and the Nasdaq frequently exceeded 0.70, signaling strong co-movement. This was not coincidence. Both assets were responding to the same macro variable: expanding liquidity.
A signal that Bitcoin had transitioned from an isolated speculative instrument to a liquidity-sensitive macro asset.


## Structural Integration, Not Speculation

For the first time in its history, Bitcoin is no longer primarily accumulated by traders, it is being systematically absorbed by institutions. That shift changes everything about how Bitcoin relates to traditional markets.

The approval of U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF in 2024 transformed Bitcoin from an asset accessed mainly through crypto-native exchanges into one embedded directly within regulated brokerage accounts. 

When capital flows into a spot ETF, the fund must acquire Bitcoin and hold it in custody. That removes supply from the open market. It reduces circulating liquidity and ties Bitcoin’s price formation more directly to institutional allocation decisions.

In April 2024, Bitcoin’s fourth halving reduced daily issuance from roughly 900 BTC per day to about 450 BTC per day. Annual new supply dropped to approximately 164,250 BTC.
At a Bitcoin price of $60,000, that annual issuance represents roughly $9.8 billion in new supply. At $70,000, it represents about $11.5 billion.

( Normally,  Annual BTC Issuance × Bitcoin Price = Dollar Value of New Annual Supply.  So if BTC is $60,000 The annual issuance will be worth $9.8 billion and vice versa )

Putting that into context: global asset managers oversee well above $100 trillion in assets. A modest 0.01% allocation shift from traditional portfolios could absorb more Bitcoin than is newly issued in a year.

This is where Bitcoin’s relationship with traditional markets becomes structurally embedded.
Bitcoin is now evaluated alongside equities, bonds, commodities, and alternatives within risk-parity frameworks and portfolio optimization models. Bitcoin is no longer adjacent to traditional finance. It sits inside it.

The transition, from traded instrument to balance-sheet allocation represents a more profound shift than price appreciation alone. It signals that Bitcoin has moved from the margins of speculation into the architecture of global capital markets.


## Bitcoin’s Influence on the Broader Crypto Market

Bitcoin does not move alone. It acts as the gravitational center of the digital asset universe.
When Bitcoin rallies, capital does not simply flow into one asset, it cascades across the broader crypto ecosystem. Historically, strong Bitcoin uptrends are followed by periods where alternative cryptocurrencies (altcoins) outperform on a percentage basis. This dynamic was visible in 2017, in 2021, and again during selective phases of 2023–2024.

Stablecoin supply also expands during bullish cycles. The total market capitalization of dollar-backed stablecoins grew from roughly $5 billion in early 2020 to over $180 billion by 2022. Stablecoins function as transactional liquidity inside the crypto ecosystem. 

As Bitcoin demand increases, so does the need for on-chain dollar equivalents to facilitate trading. Trading volumes follow the same pattern. When Bitcoin volatility rises to the upside, derivatives open interest across exchanges increases. Spot volumes across altcoins rise. Market-making spreads tighten as participation broadens. 

The reverse is equally powerful. When Bitcoin falls sharply, the broader crypto market often contracts more aggressively. Liquidity dries up. Leverage unwinds. 

Bitcoin functions as the anchor asset of the digital economy similar to how the S&P 500 anchors U.S. equity performance. 


## The Bigger Picture
Bitcoin began as a critique of the financial system. A peer-to-peer alternative designed to operate outside centralized monetary control.

Over time, something unexpected happened. Instead of remaining external to traditional finance, Bitcoin was gradually absorbed into it, not through ideological agreement, but through market demand and institutional infrastructure.

Today, Bitcoin reacts to liquidity cycles. It competes with gold narratives as a store-of-value alternative. It influences digital capital flows across exchanges and blockchain networks. It sits inside regulated investment vehicles accessible through brokerage accounts.

In periods of inflation concern, Bitcoin is compared to gold. In periods of monetary easing, it trades like a high-growth technology asset. In tightening cycles, it behaves like a risk-sensitive instrument.

The relationship between Bitcoin and traditional markets is no longer simply a matter of statistical correlation. It reflects structural integration.

Portfolio managers now ask how Bitcoin fits within asset allocation models. Regulators evaluate its role within market stability frameworks. Institutional investors analyze it alongside equities, bonds, and commodities. The dividing line between “crypto markets” and “traditional markets” grows thinner each cycle.

Bitcoin did not dismantle Wall Street. It joined it.

## The Effect of This Relationship on Tokenization
Bitcoin’s integration with traditional finance has broader implications on tokenization.
For tokenization to scale, digital asset markets must be taken seriously by institutional capital.
Bitcoin’s institutional acceptance provides that credibility. 

When pension funds allocate to Bitcoin ETFs, when regulators approve custody frameworks, and when derivatives exchange clear Bitcoin contracts, it signals that blockchain-based assets can operate within regulated financial systems.

This reduces the psychological and regulatory barrier for tokenized securities. Moreover, Bitcoin’s macro sensitivity demonstrates that digital assets can integrate into global liquidity cycles.

## Conclusion
Bitcoin’s journey from fringe experiment to macro-sensitive institutional asset reflects a deeper transformation within global finance.

It now responds to policy, liquidity conditions, and risk appetite shifts. It influences the traditional and broader market. It is embedded in regulated vehicles and institutional portfolios. Its infrastructure ties it directly to traditional market plumbing.

The relationship between Bitcoin and traditional markets is no longer about whether they are correlated in a given number of months. It is about shared capital flows, shared infrastructure, and shared macro drivers.

Bitcoin did not replace the traditional market. It became part of its architecture.

title: Saudi Arabia’s National-Scale Tokenization: A Shift Bigger Than Real Estate
content:
Saudi Arabia has taken a monumental step with the national-scale tokenization of real estate. The initiative, led by the Real Estate Registry (RER) under the Real Estate General Authority (REGA), marks the first time a nation has deployed blockchain-based property registration and fractional ownership at this scale.

Beyond the headlines, the move is significant not simply because it digitizes property records, but because of what it signals about the future of capital markets. At first glance, this may appear to be modernization of property title management: a national registry, fractional ownership, and marketplace integration. But the implications run much deeper. 

By integrating blockchain directly into the official registry and linking ownership tokens to legal title deeds, Saudi Arabia is creating an architecture where assets are legally enforceable, programmable, and globally accessible.

Imagine an institutional investor in Europe acquiring a share of a Saudi commercial property in seconds, with enforceable rights recorded directly in the national registry, without relying on intermediaries or paper-heavy processes.

Tokenization at the national level unlocks liquidity, cross-border access, and faster capital flows, while providing a clear and auditable ownership trail. For investors, this alignment between digital ownership and legal title is essential.

## Beyond Real Estate: Designing for Global Assets

The same architectural model naturally extends beyond property. Bonds, securities, stablecoins, utility tokens, and other real-world assets can all benefit from registry-anchored, compliance-native tokenization.

Cash-flow-generating assets such as royalties, infrastructure revenue streams, and other contractual income sources can be digitized into programmable financial instruments. For example, revenue from a toll road, energy project, or media rights portfolio can be tokenized, divided into discrete ownership units, and distributed according to encoded contractual rules.
Because these rules are enforced at the infrastructure level, transactions become transparent, auditable, and executable without manual reconciliation. This removes friction that normally slows cross-border investment and secondary-market trading.

For regions such as Africa, Asia, and Latin America, adopting similar infrastructure could unlock previously inaccessible pools of capital, reduce settlement friction, and enable programmable financial instruments in markets that still rely heavily on paper-based or siloed systems.

## Infrastructure Is the Real Innovation

Saudi Arabia’s initiative highlights a critical reality: the hard problem is not creating tokens. It is designing infrastructure that embeds compliance, legal enforceability, and lifecycle management from the start.

This is where platforms like Sereel become relevant. Unlike tokenization solutions that operate as overlays or require extensive retrofitting to local regulatory regimes, Sereel is built for compliance-native tokenization across multiple asset classes.

Institutions and governments can use Sereel to:

1. Issue and manage legally anchored tokenized assets, from real estate to private credit and infrastructure revenue

2. Enforce compliance rules at issuance and throughout the asset lifecycle

3. Operate across multiple chains and jurisdictions through multi-chain abstraction

4. Preserve privacy for sensitive financial relationships while remaining auditable

5. Integrate with local identity systems and capital-market infrastructure


![image](/images/blog/Sereel's_Tokenization_Infrastructur.png)

In effect, Sereel translates the lessons of national-scale initiatives like Saudi Arabia’s into modular infrastructure that can support diverse tokenized asset ecosystems.

## From Proof of Concept to Financial Infrastructure

Saudi Arabia’s launch signals that national-scale tokenization is no longer theoretical. It is operational. However, one of the quiet challenges in tokenization is that no two markets look the same. Jurisdictions impose different rules. Asset classes have different lifecycle requirements. Institutions use different technology stacks.

For institutions and governments, the central question is no longer whether tokenization is possible, but how to access infrastructure that scales with compliance, legal enforceability, and multi-asset flexibility.

Platforms such as Sereel represent the next generation of tokenization infrastructure. Built for regulatory alignment, multi-chain interoperability, and privacy where it matters, Sereel enables organizations to issue, manage, and trade tokenized assets whether real estate or not without compromising on legal or operational requirements.

The full lifecycle of an asset, from issuance to secondary-market activity, is supported within a single framework, bridging the gap between regulatory expectations and modern financial technology.

## Conclusion: A Shift Bigger Than Real Estate
Saudi Arabia’s national tokenization initiative offers a blueprint for the future. It demonstrates that the true challenge of tokenization is not the novelty of blockchain itself, but the architecture and lifecycle management of real-world assets.

Legal enforceability, compliance embedded in code, modular infrastructure, and multi-chain abstraction are becoming prerequisites for scalable, institutional-grade tokenization.

For organizations looking to tokenize assets whether at national scale or within global investment networks, adopting infrastructure that handles lifecycle management, compliance, and interoperability from day one is the only path to sustainable efficiency and trust.

For institutions exploring what this means for their own assets and markets, Sereel provides the framework to move from concept to production.

title: The hidden cost of AML/CFT: How Financial Institutions Can Lower Cost
content:
In 2024 alone, financial institutions worldwide paid over $4.5 billion in anti-money Laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) fines, with digital asset platforms like [FTX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Bankman-Fried)  facing enforcement actions totaling $12.7 billion, an unmistakable signal that compliance failures now carry existential risk.  

In recent years, financial institutions across the globe have faced staggering penalties for failing to meet AML and CFT obligations. Missteps in transaction monitoring, reporting, or sanctions screening can trigger penalties that dwarf annual profits, erode customer trust, and threaten operational resilience.

As regulators tighten their grip and financial crime grows more sophisticated, institutions now face a stark choice, either to continue absorbing spiraling compliance costs or adopt smarter, technology-driven approaches that transform compliance from a burden into a strategic & competitive advantage.

This article will examine why AML/CFT compliance has become so expensive under traditional models, how those costs disproportionately affect financial institutions, and why embedding compliance directly into financial infrastructure represents a more sustainable path forward. It explores how infrastructure-native approaches such as Sereel’s CMTAT-based token architecture can reduce compliance costs while maintaining continuous regulatory adherence across transfers and jurisdictions.

## The Current State of AML/CFT Compliance Cost

Traditional AML/CFT systems involve heavy manual processes, staff-intensive verification, and complex third-party software solutions. In developing regions like Africa, these costs often represent a larger proportion of operating budgets than in more developed markets. Between 2023 and 2024, 98% of institutions reported cost increases, with AML/CFT representing the largest share of that burden. 

In the United States and Canada alone, compliance expenditures reached $61 billion. European institutions in Germany, France, and the Netherlands collectively spend over $70 billion per year. These figures represent labor, technology, fines, and operational overhead.

![AML Market size by region](/images/blog/aml.PNG)

Compliance costs vary widely across financial institutions worldwide and high compliance costs often translate into higher fees for customers, reducing competitiveness. Africa’s per capita GDP is approximately 10 times lower than the US and UK, creating a highly price-sensitive market. 

Passing compliance costs to customers risks reducing adoption or driving clients toward non-compliant alternatives. In regions like Sub-Saharan Africa, fintechs must carefully balance regulatory adherence and market competitiveness.

Large banks in the US and Europe spend $200M+ annually on compliance, representing 2–3% of non-interest expenses, thanks to scale. However, mid-sized financial institutions in Africa, by contrast, can spend up to 8–9%, creating a competitive disadvantage.

![image](/images/blog/region_table.png)

 _Source: Federal Reserve Bank, ESAAMLG, LexisNexis, Finbold 2024_ 

These figures show that smaller institutions, particularly in Africa, bear a disproportionately higher compliance burden relative to operational size. This disparity arises because regulatory requirements are largely uniform regardless of institution size, leaving smaller banks and fintechs with fewer economies of scale.

By contrast, large banks in the EU and US manage compliance more efficiently due to advanced technological infrastructure and automation. While penalties can be lower in Africa in absolute terms, their impact relative to institutional size is higher, often threatening operational viability.

Compliance failures divert staff time, increase auditing costs, and can halt operations. In Africa, institutions report up to 50% of staff time allocated to AML reporting and remediation, versus 30% in developed markets, reflecting resource constraints.

Non-compliance erodes customer trust and investor confidence and  reputational risk is amplified. A fintech with a delayed compliance report can lose a significant portion of its clients overnight.

## The High Cost of Non-Compliance: Beyond Fines and Penalties

While regulatory fines often dominate headlines, the true cost of AML/CFT non-compliance extends far beyond monetary penalties. Financial institutions that fall short of regulatory expectations face cascading consequences that affect operations, growth, and long-term sustainability.

Regulators across the world have increasingly adopted a zero-tolerance stance toward AML/CFT failures. Institutions like [TD Bank was penalized over $3.1 billion](https://thefinancialcrimenews.com/bank-fi-aml-sanctions-fines-penalties-in-the-21st-century/) for significant failures in its AML compliance program, marking one of the largest AML-related penalties ever imposed on a financial institution. Similarly [Metro Bank was fined £16.7 million by the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA)](https://www.fca.org.uk/news/press-releases/fca-fines-metro-bank-16m-financial-crime-failings) for serious weaknesses in its transaction monitoring systems and FTX, a digital asset exchange was ordered to pay $12.7 billion in enforcement actions tied to fraud and compliance failures.

These cases demonstrate that AML/CFT enforcement now applies uniformly across financial institutions, whether they operate in traditional banking, fintech, or digital asset ecosystems. 
Beyond fines, enforcement actions often trigger costly remediation programs. Institutions may be required to:
- Hire independent compliance monitors

- Redesign AML frameworks

- Upgrade transaction monitoring systems

- Retrain staff

- Submit to multi-year regulatory oversight

In many cases, remediation costs exceed the original fine itself. For smaller institutions, particularly in emerging markets, these requirements can stretch operational capacity to breaking point.

In Africa, regulatory remediation often involves manual backfilling of compliance gaps, extensive reporting, and increased scrutiny from local and international regulators. This can delay product launches, slow transaction processing, and restrict cross-border operations, directly impacting revenue.

Compliance failures also carry significant reputational risk. Trust is the foundation of financial services, and once lost, it is difficult to rebuild.

In developed markets, large institutions may absorb reputational damage through brand strength and diversified customer bases. In contrast, financial institutions and fintechs often operate in smaller, highly competitive markets, where reputational setbacks can lead to rapid customer churn.

A single compliance lapse can trigger customer withdrawals or discourage institutional partners

## Why Traditional AML/CFT Models Are No Longer Sustainable

The global compliance landscape has shifted. Traditional AML/CFT frameworks built around post-transaction monitoring, fragmented systems, and human-intensive processes are struggling to keep pace with rising transaction volumes, tokenized financial instruments and cross-border digital asset transfers.

This mismatch between legacy compliance infrastructure and modern financial activity is driving costs upward while increasing regulatory risk.

For financial institutions operating across both traditional finance and decentralized infrastructure, the question is no longer whether compliance is necessary but how to achieve it efficiently, consistently, and at scale.

This challenge has created an urgent need for compliance-native financial infrastructure, systems where AML/CFT controls are embedded directly into the assets and transactions themselves, rather than layered on as an afterthought.

Perhaps the most damaging issue is how compliance is positioned internally. In many institutions, AML/CFT is still viewed as regulatory obligation, a defensive function, and necessary expense to avoid fines. When compliance is treated purely as a cost center, institutions invest only enough to “meet requirements,” rather than building systems that improve operational efficiency and strengthen trust with partners and regulators.

In contrast, institutions that embed compliance into their core infrastructure rather than layering it on top are better positioned to scale securely, especially in emerging financial models like tokenization and onchain finance.

## Reducing the Cost of Compliance: Sereel’s CMTAT Infrastructure

Rising AML/CFT compliance costs are a growing burden for financial institutions and fintechs. AML and CFT compliance has been treated as a separate operational layer, something financial institutions “add on” after transactions are executed. This approach has proven expensive, inefficient, and increasingly unsustainable. As enforcement actions rise and financial crime becomes more sophisticated, the cost of maintaining compliance through fragmented tools, manual reviews, and post-transaction monitoring continues to climb.

Sereel takes a fundamentally different approach. Rather than positioning compliance as an external control mechanism, Sereel embeds AML/CFT compliance directly into the financial infrastructure itself. By integrating regulatory logic at the token and transaction level, compliance is enforced by design, not by after-the-fact intervention. This shift alone has profound cost implications for financial institutions.

At the core of Sereel’s architecture is the implementation of the **CMTAT (Capital Markets and Technology Association Token)** standard within tokenized assets. This means that compliance requirement such as allowlisting, account freezing, transfer restrictions, and auditability are not managed through disconnected compliance software or manual processes. They are natively embedded into the asset’s lifecycle from issuance to transfer.

In practical terms, this removes the need for multiple layers of transaction screening and repetitive verification checks that traditionally inflate AML/CFT budgets. When compliance rules are enforced automatically at the infrastructure level, financial institutions spend significantly less on monitoring tools, third-party vendors, and compliance headcount dedicated to remediation.

A major cost driver in traditional AML systems is the reliance on post-transaction monitoring. Transactions are processed first, flagged later, reviewed manually, and escalated across compliance team, often across multiple jurisdictions. This model not only increases operational cost but also introduces regulatory risk.

Sereel replaces this model with pre-emptive and continuous compliance. Because CMTAT-compliant tokens can restrict transfers to verified and allowlisted participants, non-compliant transactions are prevented before they occur.

This approach drastically reduces false positives: one of the most expensive inefficiencies in AML operations globally. Industry studies estimate that over 90% of AML alerts are false positives, consuming thousands of staff hours annually. 

Cost reduction also extends to cross-border and secondary transfers, where AML/CFT complexity typically increases. In traditional systems, every transfer introduces new compliance checks, new intermediaries, and additional reporting obligations. Each step adds cost including intermediary charges.

With Sereel, compliance persists across transfers. Because CMTAT rules are embedded directly into the token, regulatory controls travel with the asset regardless of how many times it changes hands or across which networks it moves. This persistence eliminates the need for repeated onboarding, re-verification, and redundant monitoring, significantly lowering cumulative compliance costs over the asset’s lifetime.

Another overlooked cost in AML/CFT operations is remediation. When suspicious activity is detected in legacy systems, institutions often have limited options beyond account suspension, lengthy investigations, or regulatory reporting. These processes are slow, resource-intensive, and reputationally risky.

Sereel introduces a more controlled and cost-efficient alternative. In cases of suspected foul play, issuers retain the ability to freeze or force-transfer tokens in line with regulatory requirements. This capability allows institutions to act decisively without halting entire operations or triggering system-wide compliance reviews. The result is faster resolution, lower investigation costs, and reduced exposure to regulatory penalties.

Importantly, Sereel’s infrastructure-level compliance also reduces long-term technology costs. Traditional AML stacks often rely on transaction monitoring providers, sanctions screening tools, identity verification platforms, and reporting systems. Maintaining and integrating these tools accounts for a substantial portion of annual compliance budgets.

By consolidating compliance enforcement into the token and transaction infrastructure itself, Sereel reduces dependency on external systems. This simplification lowers licensing fees, integration costs, and ongoing maintenance expenses, particularly for fintechs and mid-sized financial institutions that lack the economies of scale enjoyed by global banks.

In an environment where compliance costs are rising faster than revenue growth, this architectural shift is not merely an efficiency gain but a strategic necessity. By embedding AML/CFT compliance directly into financial infrastructure, Sereel enables institutions to meet regulatory expectations while materially lowering operational, technological, and human costs.

Rather than asking institutions to choose between compliance and competitiveness, Sereel demonstrates how both can coexist with compliance built into the system from the ground up.![image](/images/blog/Category_table.png)

## Conclusion

AML/CFT compliance remains a high-cost, high-stakes challenge for financial institutions worldwide. While banks in the US and EU have the infrastructure to manage costs efficiently, financial institutions in regions like Africa face unique challenges: fragmented regulation, informal economies, high staff burdens, and price-sensitive markets.

Sereel’s CMTAT token architecture provides a transformative, automated, and scalable solution, reducing compliance costs, mitigating risk, and ensuring persistent adherence to AML/CFT regulations. By leveraging this technology, financial institutions can maintain competitive advantage, protect their operations, and meet regulatory obligations, all while lowering operational costs.

title: The Falcon Leap: Redefining Digital Signatures Beyond Classical Cryptography
content:
Classical cryptography is not broken, it’s simply on a clock.

For decades, digital signatures based on number-theoretic algorithms like DSA and RSA have secured systems, identity layers, institutional infrastructure. They continue to function exactly as intended. They are still trusted and secure. They still work. They are still safe... for now.

![image](/images/blog/Encryption_2.jpg)

The reason is simple: all of them are based on mathematical problems impossible for classical computers to solve within any reasonable timeframe. However, these same assumptions do not hold in the presence of large-scale quantum computers. 

Quantum computing introduces a fundamentally different computational model, forcing cryptography to evolve rather than react. These models change the cost of solving the hard problems classical cryptography depends on. 

This does not mean classical cryptographic systems are failing today. It means the margin of safety that encryptions currently rely on is finite. When quantum computer becomes fully operational , the mathematics that runs today’s systems becomes fully cracked like an egg, invalidating  much of the current public-key cryptography overnight.

While building the quantum machine is still huge technical challenge, the existence of a fully functional quantum machines capable of threatening today’s public-key systems can evaporate the current security model, and this creates a critical reality: the time to upgrade number-based theorectic algorithm systems is not when quantum computers arrive, but long before they do. 

The real question is not whether post-quantum cryptography: a class of algorithms designed to resist both classical and quantum attacks will be necessary, but whether systems being built today are designed to survive that transition without disruption.

## Why Quantum Computing Changes the Rules of Cryptography

Classical cryptography relies on mathematical problems that are practically impossible for conventional computers to solve. Public-key digital signatures, such as RSA, DSA, and ECDSA, depend on the difficulty of factoring large numbers or computing discrete logarithms.
 
Quantum computing, however, changes the rules. The secret is moving from number theory to geometry. Unlike classical bits, quantum computing uses qubits which can exist in multiple states simultaneously; a property known as [superposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_superposition) and can interact through entanglement. This allows quantum computers to perform calculations in parallel, making certain problems exponentially faster to solve.

Two quantum algorithms exemplify this threat:

- Shor’s algorithm: Efficiently factors large integers and computes discrete logarithms, directly undermining RSA, DSA, and ECDSA.

- Grover’s algorithm: Accelerates brute-force attacks, reducing the security of symmetric key systems.

What was once considered computationally infeasible becomes realistically solvable on a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. In effect, quantum computing does not weaken cryptography; it removes the mathematical hardness those systems depend on.

While today’s quantum computers are not yet capable of breaking real-world encryption, the risk is already present. Encrypted data can be collected now and decrypted later when quantum hardware matures, a strategy known as “harvest now, decrypt later.” This makes long-term security a pressing concern.

In the instance of blockchain, quantum computing poses a fundamental risk to signatures, because they prove ownership, authorize transactions, and secure consensus. On Bitcoin alone, over 460 million BTC addresses rely on elliptic-curve cryptography for transaction signing. These signatures remain secure today, but quantum computing will change the rules in the near future.

A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could recover private keys from publicly visible on-chain keys. This would allow attackers to forge signatures, impersonate owners or validators, and authorize fraudulent transactions. Unlike traditional systems, blockchains are especially exposed because their data is permanent and public. Keys revealed today may remain attackable far into the future. This makes long-lived wallets, treasuries, multisigs, and core protocol contracts particularly vulnerable over time.

Consider a multisig treasury managing over $500M in tokenized assets. With classical cryptography, unauthorized transactions are practically impossible. With a large-scale quantum computer, algorithms like Shor’s could theoretically derive the private keys from public addresses, allowing attackers to authorize transfers undetected.

Even though quantum computers are not yet capable of executing these attacks, the “harvest now, exploit later” risk already applies. Data, keys, and signatures exposed today may be analyzed and compromised in the future once quantum capabilities mature. 

As a result, systems must be designed with change in mind. Prioritizing cryptographic upgradeability, key rotation, abstraction layers, and forward compatibility with quantum-resistant signature schemes such as Falcon, Dilithium, or SPHINCS+ is no longer a forward-looking enhancement, but a baseline requirement for long-lived security.

This brings us to post-quantum cryptography.

Post-quantum cryptography does not attempt to forecast when large-scale quantum computers will arrive. Instead, it assumes their eventual existence and focuses on designing cryptographic algorithms that remain secure even under quantum adversaries. Importantly, post-quantum cryptography is not a single algorithm or approach. It is a broader class of cryptographic constructions, each built on mathematical problems that are believed to resist both classical and quantum attacks.

## What Post-Quantum Means in the Context of Digital Signatures

With classical cryptography on borrowed time under the looming threat of quantum computing, digital signatures in both traditional systems and blockchain networks face a critical challenge.

A 2023 NIST report notes that large-scale quantum computers capable of breaking elliptic-curve signatures could exist within 15–20 years, making long-term key security a real concern today.

![image](/images/blog/NIST.png)

Post-quantum cryptography redefines what a secure signature must deliver. Unlike classical schemes, which derive their security from number-theoretic hardness, post-quantum signatures are constructed on problems believed to resist quantum attacks. 

One of such is Lattice-based signatures where security relies on the geometric complexity of high-dimensional lattices, such as finding short vectors hidden in a lattice. This approach offers strong security proofs and practical efficiency for verification, signing, and storage.

For digital signatures in blockchains, long-term tokenized assets, multisignature wallets, and institutional ledgers, these differences matter. Signatures are not just proofs of ownership; they authorize actions, validate transactions, and maintain consensus. Their performance, size, and verifiability directly impact throughput, scalability, and user experience.

Imagine a real estate token  like bonds and debts issued today and might be locked on-chain for the next 10–15 years, classical cryptography puts the asset at risk once quantum computers mature. Lattice-based signatures, like Falcon, ensure that the proof of ownership remains secure, regardless of future computational advances and without requiring constant system-wide upgrades.

The takeaway is clear: post-quantum signatures are not a distant concern. They are a design imperative for any system intended to endure, scale, and remain trustworthy over the coming years. Building cryptographic agility and designing systems with layered architectures that allow classical signatures to coexist with quantum-resistant schemes should be a top priority. 

This approach ensures that blockchain networks, tokenized assets, and institutional ledgers remain secure, verifiable, and operationally efficient today and continue to do so in a post-quantum future.

## Falcon Algorithm:  A Modern Post-Quantum Cryptographic Algorithm

In 2024, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)  finalized selection of its principal set of encryption algorithms designed to withstand attacks from a quantum computer. Falcon was one of the approved post-quantum digital encryption standards. 

On August 28, 2025, NIST submitted the draft standard for FN-DSA (FIPS 206) for approval. FN-DSA is NIST’s official name for the FALCON-based Digital Signature Algorithm based on FALCON, selected alongside Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm ( ML-DSA) and Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA)  for post-quantum standardization.

Falcon is an acronym for “fast Fourier lattice-based compact signatures over NTRU”, a lattice-based digital signature scheme designed from the ground up to remain secure against both classical and quantum adversaries while producing compact signatures and fast verification, even under heavy load.

![image](/images/blog/falcon.png)

Unlike RSA or ECDSA, Falcon does not rely on the hardness of factoring large integers or solving discrete logarithms. Instead, it belongs to a family of lattice-based cryptography, a field pioneered in the late 1990s and early 2000s and now widely regarded as one of the most promising foundations for post-quantum security.

At a high level, Falcon replaces number-theoretic assumptions with geometric ones. Unlike classical cryptography that asks questions like, can you factor this enormous number? Or can you recover a private key from a public key on an elliptic curve? Quantum computers are exceptionally good at these problems. 

Falcon moves the security problem into a space where quantum computers gain little to no advantage. Its security is rooted in the difficulty of navigating high-dimensional lattices: mathematical structures that can be visualized as extremely complex, multi-dimensional grids of points. Not a flat grid, but one with hundreds of dimensions, dense structure, and no obvious paths.

In this world, breaking a signature is no longer about brute force or clever factoring. It’s about solving a geometric problem that remains hard even with quantum acceleration.

## The Core Security Engine: NTRU Lattices and SIS

Falcon is built using a specific lattice structure known as NTRU lattices, defined over polynomial rings. This design choice gives Falcon two critical advantages:
- Speed: Polynomial ring operations enable efficient computation using Fast Fourier Transforms.
- Compactness: Keys and signatures are significantly smaller than many other post-quantum alternatives.

Under the hood, Falcon’s security relies on a well-studied hard problem called Short Integer Solution (SIS). In simple terms, the SIS problem asks: Given a complex lattice, can you find a short, non-zero vector that satisfies a specific equation?

As lattice dimensions grow, this becomes extraordinarily difficult. Even with quantum computers, there is no known efficient method to solve SIS at the scales Falcon operates.
Falcon moves cryptographic security away from problem spaces where quantum computers excel, and into one where their advantage is negligible.

You can think of this as a cryptographic firewall engine redirecting attacks into terrain where they stall rather than accelerate. Why does this matter in Practice?

Consider a tokenized asset such as a bond, real estate instrument, or long-term debt issued today and locked on-chain for 10 to 15 years. With classical signatures, the asset is secure only as long as elliptic-curve assumptions hold. Once quantum computers mature, historical public keys become liabilities. 

However, with Falcon, that risk profile changes; security does not degrade under quantum models, a Falcon-signed asset can remain verifiable without emergency migrations, chain-wide key rotations, or retroactive invalidation of ownership proofs.

Similarly, a multisignature treasury managing hundreds of millions in digital assets benefits from Falcon’s compact signatures and efficient verification. Transactions remain fast, and network throughput is maintained while achieving post-quantum security. 

This makes Falcon particularly suitable for environments where both performance and security are critical. Because its security does not degrade under quantum models, a Falcon-signed asset can remain verifiable without emergency migrations, chain-wide key rotations, or retroactive invalidation of ownership proofs.

In these post quantum algorithms, signature size, verification speed, and long-term survivability are not optional, they are foundational. By combining strong security with operational efficiency, Falcon provides a blueprint for how post-quantum signatures can be practically deployed today, ensuring long-term protection for sensitive systems, blockchain networks, and tokenized assets.

## How Falcon creates a signature

At a high level, creating a Falcon signature means finding a short vector in a lattice that satisfies a specific equation. This vector must:

- Be valid for verification
- Be statistically independent of the secret key
- Be sampled efficiently
 
Naively sampling short vectors in high-dimensional lattices is slow and computationally intensive. Worse, repeated sampling can accidentally introduce tiny correlations between the signatures and the private key.Those correlations are dangerous.

Over time, they can be exploited through side-channel or statistical attacks, even if the underlying math remains sound. Falcon’s design solves both problems of speed and leakage at the same time.

## Fast Fourier Sampling  

Fast Fourier Sampling  is where Falcon distinguishes itself. Instead of operating directly on lattice vectors in the time domain, Falcon works in the frequency domain using Fast Fourier Sampling.

Concretely, Falcon relies on the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), a lattice-friendly analogue of the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). The idea is simple but powerful, Polynomial operations that would normally cost:

**O(n²)**

are transformed into:

**O(n log n)**

The transform converts complex polynomial arithmetic into fast, element-wise multiplications, then transforms the result back. This is the secret behind Falcon’s performance.
Rather than fighting the complexity of the lattice, Falcon reshapes the problem into a form where modern hardware excels. Signature generation becomes fast enough for real-time systems, while verification becomes even faster.

This is why Falcon can generate thousands of signatures per second on standard hardware, despite being built on deep lattice mathematics.

## Gaussian Sampling: Preventing Information Leakage

Speed alone is not enough. A fast but leaky signature scheme is worse than no scheme at all.
Every digital signature algorithm faces a risk: even if each individual signature looks safe, tiny statistical biases can accumulate. Over many signatures, those biases can reveal information about the private key.

Falcon addresses this using true discrete Gaussian sampling.
Instead of producing signatures with predictable structure, Falcon samples signature vectors from a carefully tuned Gaussian distribution over the lattice. Mathematically, this ensures that:
- Each signature is statistically independent
- Correlations with the secret key vanish exponentially
- Leakage remains negligible, even after an enormous number of signatures

In practice, this means Falcon can safely sign more than **2⁶⁴** messages without meaningful risk of key exposure.
This property is critical for blockchains, validators, and institutional systems where keys may be used continuously over many years.

Why This Matters

Falcon’s signature process is not just clever, it is deliberate.
- Fast Fourier sampling makes lattice operations practical
- NTT-based computation unlocks real-world performance
- Gaussian sampling neutralizes side-channel leakage
- Security remains intact under both classical and quantum models
This is what allows Falcon to bridge the gap between hard post-quantum mathematics and deployable cryptography.

## Performance, Global Adoption, and Tradeoff of Falcon 

Falcon’s strength lies first in its compact signatures, which are significantly smaller than other lattice-based alternatives at the same security level. In blockchain systems where every transaction, validator vote, or cross-chain message carries a signature, smaller sizes reduce bandwidth usage, block size pressure, and long-term storage costs. For instance, a high-volume rollup processing thousands of transactions per minute benefits from this efficiency, avoiding unnecessary network congestion.

This efficiency comes with a conscious tradeoff: Falcon’s public keys are moderately larger than classical schemes like RSA or ECDSA. In practice, this is negligible because public keys are generated once and stored, while signatures are continuously transmitted. Institutional custody platforms or validator infrastructures gain ongoing savings from fast, small signatures, making the slightly larger key size a small price to pay.

Overall, Falcon achieves one of the best signature-to-key size ratios among post-quantum schemes. By accepting slightly larger public keys, it delivers extremely small signatures, a critical advantage for bandwidth-sensitive environments. In cross-chain bridges or messaging-heavy layer-2 networks, the cumulative savings from smaller signatures quickly outweigh the one-time cost of storing larger keys, making Falcon optimal for such scenarios.

Falcon also delivers real-world speed, thanks to Fast Fourier sampling and polynomial arithmetic. Signature generation reaches thousands per second on standard consumer hardware, with verification five to ten times faster. High-throughput systems such as blockchain validators, payment rails, or tokenized asset networks depend on verification speed; any slowdown would create bottlenecks, but Falcon avoids this entirely.

The numbers back it up: Falcon-512, which provides classical security comparable to RSA-2048, achieves roughly 6,000 key generations per second, 5,000 signatures per second, and 27,000 verifications per second. These metrics make Falcon suitable for production-grade systems, from large-scale stablecoin issuers to institutional treasuries managing hundreds of millions in digital assets.

Beyond performance, standardization and early adoption reinforce Falcon’s readiness. NIST selection signals cryptographic confidence, and implementations already exist in Python and blockchain platforms like Algorand. This shows that Falcon is not just theoretical. It’s being tested and deployed in real-world systems.

## Conclusion

Falcon represents a balanced set of tradeoffs, rather than a one-size-fits-all solution. Its design prioritizes compact signatures, fast verification, low memory usage, and long-term quantum resistance, while accepting slightly larger public keys and a more complex implementation. For systems where durability, verification speed, and bandwidth efficiency matter more than absolute simplicity, these tradeoffs are not compromises, they are practical design choices aligned with real operational needs.

title: Ethereum Fusaka Upgrade
content:
## Fusaka is Live

Today, December 3rd at 21:49 UTC, Ethereum activates Fusaka: the network's second hard fork of 2025 and one of the most consequential in terms of efficiency and scalability. The name combines Fulu, a star in the Cassiopeia constellation, with Osaka, the Japanese city where Devcon V was held. Fulu is the upgrade to the Ethereum consensus layer, Osaka is the upgrade on the execution layer. Together they create Fusaka. 

In this blog post, we'll explore the Fusaka upgrade on a high level and dive deep into an upgrade that impacts Sereel tremendously.

## The Fusaka Upgrade

The Fusaka Upgrade has several improvements (see figure below), but the most known is PeerDAS, which stands for Peer Data Availability Sampling.

![image](/images/blog/Fusaka_1.png)

PeerDAS is Ethereum's answer to a fundamental constraint: how do you increase data availability without forcing every node to download everything?

The previous model was simple, but unsustainable. Every full node had to store every blob, you can think of blobs as data storage units for transactions rolled up on a Layer 2 (L2) blockchain. As L2 usage exploded post-Dencun (the fork that introduced EIP4844 Proto-dank sharding), Ethereum users started hitting the 9-blob-per-block ceiling regularly. PeerDAS changes the architecture: instead of downloading 100% of blob data, each node now holds about 1/8th. Erasure coding guarantees that any 50% of the distributed data can reconstruct the rest. In turn, the reconstruction failure probability drops to somewhere between one in 10²⁰ and one in 10²⁴.

For L2s, this means cheaper fees and higher throughput without compromising security. Blob Parameter Only forks mean Ethereum can now adjust these parameters without waiting for full hard forks. The blob target will increase from 6 to 10 in BPO1 (December 9th), then to 14 in BPO2 (January 7th, 2026). 

## Sereel's Use for EIP-7951

There are a myriad of upgrades in Fusaka: the gas limit increases to 60M enabling for more transactions with greater complexity. Block time consumption issues are fixed with ModExp gas repricing. However, for Sereel, we're extremely excited about EIP-7951: the secp256r1 precompile at address 0x100. We've been following developments on this precompile since [RIP-7212](https://github.com/ethereum/RIPs/blob/master/RIPS/rip-7212.md). We're so excited to see it on mainnet!

secp256r1 is the elliptic curve used by basically every piece of secure hardware on the market: Apple's Secure Enclave, Android Keystore, FIDO2/WebAuthn devices, YubiKeys, HSMs, you name it. Ethereum has historically used secp256k1. This is the Koblitz curve that Satoshi Nakamoto chose for Bitcoin. The "k" stands for Koblitz, the "r" stands for random, referring to the NIST randomization of the curve parameters.

![image](/images/blog/Fusaka_2.PNG)

Why does the curve matter? Because until now, verifying a secp256r1 (R1) signature on Ethereum required expensive smart contract choreography. The best Solidity R1 verifier was developed by Daimo in 2023. It costs around 330,000 (as much as $14 with high network activity) gas on mainnet for a single signature verification. Prohibitively expensive. Daunting when selling to institutions that want access to mainnet's liquidity. EIP-7951 drops that to 6,900 gas. That's an approximate 98% reduction. Pennies on mainnet.

## Our Experience with secp256r1

Our co-founder, Lance, was there at [Zuzalu](https://www.zuzalu.city/) when the Daimo team first unveiled the secp256r1 verifier. It was built specifically for mobile passkeys for their consumer stablecoin wallet. Sereel co-founders spent countless hours studying the implementation to modify it for its non-custodial wallet desktop app. 

The need for solid secp256r1 verification is widespread. Traditional crypto custody relies on seed phrases and externally-owned accounts secured by secp256k1 keys. This works fine for retail, but poses serious problems for institutions. How do you achieve the kind of hardware-backed security that regulated financial institutions expect? Even consumer apps like Daimo used R1 for ease of use and security.

The solution was to create an ERC4337 smart wallet that used an R1 signature for verification rather than a K1 signature. Despite the gas overhead, on an L2 it was bearable and gained a serious level of adoption. Other applications like Clave and Onboard used this signature scheme to reduce barriers for their stablecoin payment apps. 

## Using WebAuthn on Sereel

Our work with secp256r1 didn’t end at research or remained theoretical. Everything we learned with Daimo’s verifier shaped how we modified Sereel’s authentication stack. This evolution leads naturally to one of Sereel’s most powerful capabilities today: native WebAuthn support for hardware-backed institutional wallets. 

When creating an institutional wallet / multisig on Sereel, you can use your mobile device, your laptop, or a separate YubiKey for wallet creation and transaction authentication. With Sereel, you can securely use your hardware key for non-EVM wallets as well, such as Bitcoin or Starknet.

The infrastructure layer is scaling fast and Sereel is equipped for this new phase. We are here to keep you ahead and secure. 

Reach out to the Sereel team to learn how hardware-backed custody can work for your fund.
